extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, critics, and practitioners interested in the theory and mechanics of humor (literary critics, playwrights, comedians interested in comic theory)
extracted.subtask_description: Philosophical/literary analysis of what makes things laughable: the special forms of absurdity, the peculiar 'logic' of comic figures, dream-like mechanisms, and the social function of laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particular kind of absurdity
rubrics_metrics.description: Absurdity, when met with in the comic, is not absurdity IN GENERAL. It is an absurdity of a definite kind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General definitions that equate the comic with 'the absurd' fail because they ignore the particular nature of the comic's absurdity; the comic 'infuses into' an absurdity its own particular essence. Attempting to manufacture comic effects by using 'absurdity in general' will often fail ("twice out of every three times there will be nothing laughable"). Example contrast: ordinary absurdity vs. the comic absurdity exemplified by Don Quixote.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logic peculiar to the comic character or group (professional logic)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is such a thing as a professional logic—certain ways of reasoning customary in certain circles—which are valid for these circles but untrue for the rest of the public; the contrast between this particular logic and universal logic produces comic effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comic often arises from the clash between a specialised, internally-consistent logic and common-sense logic. Example: translations of scientific ideas into 'feminine sensibility' in Moliere's Femmes savantes; 'professional' modes of reasoning that seem absurd to outsiders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obstinate adherence to a single idea / automatism
rubrics_metrics.description: The comic character always errs through obstinacy of mind or disposition, through absentmindedness, in short, through automatism—'A CHARACTER FOLLOWING UP HIS ONE IDEA, and continually recurring to it in spite of incessant interruptions!'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many comic scenes reduce to a character rigidly following one line of thought or behavior; this rigidity leads the character to adjust reality to their idea instead of adjusting ideas to reality (Don Quixote as archetype). Example: repeated insistence on a point despite contrary evidence in Moliere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privileged recollection dominating perception (moulding things on an idea)
rubrics_metrics.description: A privileged recollection or idea can take command of perception so that we 'mould things on an idea of one's own, instead of moulding one's ideas on things' (Don Quixote sees giants where others see windmills).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comic effect arises when memory or an idea is privileged and imposed on the world, producing a systematic mis-recognition; once the illusion is created, the character develops it 'logically enough' and acts with the precision of a somnambulist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic absurdity akin to dream-logic
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic absurdity is of the same nature as that of dreams.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The mind in dreams uses perception as a pretext to realize its imaginations; similarly, comic characters appeal to partial recollections or favored ideas to interpret perceptions. Therefore, many features of dream-logic (reduced tension, fusion of identities, weird concatenations) are characteristic of the comic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relaxation of the rules of reasoning / abridged reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: The reasonings at which we laugh are those we know to be false, but which we might accept as true were we to hear them in a dream—reasonings lacking in tension or considerably abridged (we are given only the beginning and the end).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comic reasoning counterfeits true reasoning just enough to deceive a mind 'dropping off to sleep'; such abridgement relieves intellectual effort and produces amusement. Many witticisms are of this structural type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Play upon words from superficial idea-relations
rubrics_metrics.description: As the relations set up between ideas become more superficial, play upon ideas evolves into play upon words; we come to take no account of meaning but only of sound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When semantic connections are shallow, comic effect often shifts to phonetic or verbal play. Examples: dreams where speech becomes distorted and recombines into strange meanings; stage scenes where whispered nonsense is repeated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic obsessions and repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: COMIC OBSESSIONS resemble dream obsessions: the same image or phrase recurs in successive scenes/verses, assuming a plausible but shifting meaning each time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repetition can produce comic effects by recurring unchanged yet reinterpreted; examples include song burdens repeated at each verse with different meanings, or recurring images across dreams and scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crescendo toward absurdity / progressive intensification
rubrics_metrics.description: A particular crescendo often occurs: the first concession to absurdity introduces a second, then another, until the crowning absurdity is reached.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This progressive drift into absurdity produces a peculiar sensation (analogous to a tippler drifting into blankness). Examples: Moliere's Monsieur de Pourceaugnac and The Bourgeois gentilhomme, where the plays begin reasonably and escalate into extravagant absurdities until the audience is 'roused' out of the dream.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confusion or fusion of identities
rubrics_metrics.description: Dreams often fuse two persons into one who is simultaneously distinct and identical (the dreamer 'is himself, and not himself'); similar extraordinary confusions appear in comic scenes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comic effect can stem from perspective shifts or narratorial confusion where a speaker treats themselves as both actor and observer. Example: Mark Twain's interview dialogue where the speaker oscillates between being one of the twins and describing them as a third person, producing a specialized absurdity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughter as corrective and humiliating (social function)
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter is, above all, a corrective. Being intended to humiliate, it must make a painful impression on the person against whom it is directed; by laughter society avenges itself for liberties taken with it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laughter functions like social punishment—often not benevolent or perfectly just—and serves to check and coerce behavior. The comic types are 'models of impertinence' that society 'retorts by laughter'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initial sympathetic invitation to 'take it easy' followed by punitive distance
rubrics_metrics.description: The comic character often elicits a brief sympathy (we 'put ourselves... in his place' and join the play), but this sympathy is fleeting; laughter then withdraws and humiliates the target.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is an initial relaxation and shared playfulness (relief from the strain of living), but the laugher soon 'retires within himself' and adopts a superior, punitive stance—indicating laughter's ambivalent nature (playful then corrective).

rubrics_metrics.name: Spontaneity of laughter; collective averaging rather than individual justice
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter is simply the result of a mechanism set up in us by nature or by our long acquaintance with social life; it goes off spontaneously and has no time to look where it hits—striking down some innocent and sparing some guilty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because laughter is automatic rather than reflective, it cannot be absolutely just; its function may yield a beneficial average outcome for society even while erring at the level of individual cases. This explains both its effectiveness and its cruelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic as impertinence that reveals social undulations
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic types are models of impertinence with regard to society; laughter emphasises the form of these significant undulations on the surface of social life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Like waves clashing on the sea's surface while depths remain peaceful, laughter highlights surface disturbances—brief, frothy, and sometimes bitter in after-taste—thus policing social norms by making impertinences visible and laughable.
